terminal.description: A shell in your workspace: node run.mjs <file> runs the query in that file against a fresh copy of the practice's database and prints the rows.

tasks.title: Sort the phone book by surname
tasks.description:
Winnie wants the owners in the same order as the paper cards: by surname, A to Z.

In `queries/1-phone-book.sql`, return three columns from `owners`, in this order:

- `last_name`
- `first_name`
- `phone`

Every owner, sorted by `last_name` from A to Z. Check compares the columns, the rows and their order on the data you can see and on hidden data.
nextSteps: Write the query with the three columns and run it. Look at the order the rows come back in.
Add the part that sorts the rows, after `FROM`.
Run it again and read down the surnames: A at the top, Z at the bottom.
hints: Without a sort, rows come back in whatever order SQLite finds them. The lesson's part "Putting rows in order" shows how to ask for one.
`ORDER BY` goes at the end of the query and takes the column to sort by. A to Z is the order it uses when you say nothing else.
The last line has the shape `ORDER BY column;`, with the column name written without quotes.

tasks.title: List the dogs, heaviest first
tasks.description:
Ifan doses worming tablets by weight and works down from the biggest dog.

In `queries/2-heaviest-dogs.sql`, return two columns from `animals`, in this order:

- `name`
- `weight_kg`

Only dogs, sorted by `weight_kg` from the heaviest to the lightest. A dog nobody has weighed yet goes at the very end. Check compares the columns, the rows and their order on the data you can see and on hidden data.
nextSteps: Write a query that returns the two columns for the dogs only, and run it.
Sort it by weight and run it. Which end is the heaviest dog at?
Turn the sort around so the heaviest dog is first.
Find the dog with no weight. Is it where the task wants it?
hints: This query needs the `WHERE` from earlier issues and a sort, in that order.
A sort runs from the smallest to the largest unless you say otherwise. One word after the column turns it around.
The end of the query has the shape `WHERE species = '...' ORDER BY column DESC;`. Run it and check where the dog with no weight lands.

tasks.title: Sort the visits by vet, newest first
tasks.description:
Rosamund is reviewing each vet's recent work and wants every visit, one vet at a time.

In `queries/3-visits-by-vet.sql`, return three columns from `visits`, in this order:

- `vet`
- `visit_date`
- `reason`

Every visit, sorted by `vet` from A to Z, and within each vet by `visit_date` with the newest visit first. Check compares the columns, the rows and their order on the data you can see and on hidden data.
nextSteps: Write the query with the three columns and sort it by vet. Run it and look at the dates inside each vet.
Add a second column to the sort, so the dates inside each vet are in order.
Check the direction of each column: vets A to Z, dates newest first.
hints: A sort can take more than one column. The second one only decides the order of rows that tie on the first.
Each column in the sort has its own direction. `DESC` after one column does not change the other.
The last line has the shape `ORDER BY first_column, second_column DESC;`.

tasks.title: Find the three oldest animals
tasks.description:
Winnie writes to the owners of the oldest animals about a senior health check, three letters at a time.

In `queries/4-oldest-three.sql`, return three columns from `animals`, in this order:

- `name`
- `species`
- `born`

The three animals born earliest, oldest first. Leave out animals whose birthday nobody knows. When two animals were born on the same day, the one whose `name` comes first from A to Z goes first. Check compares the columns, the rows and their order on the data you can see and on hidden data, which has its own tie.
nextSteps: Sort every animal by `born` and run it without a limit. Look at the top of the list.
Deal with the animals whose birthday is missing, so they are not at the top.
Find the two animals born on the same day, and make the sort say which comes first.
Keep only the first three rows.
hints: Run the sort without a limit first and read the top rows. The lesson's part "Where empty cells go" explains what you see.
Leave out the missing birthdays with a condition you know, or move them to the end of the sort. Then add a second column to the sort for the tie.
The query ends with the shape `ORDER BY born, name LIMIT 3;`, and the missing birthdays are dealt with before that.
